question: Recent geopolitical tensions in Iran are once again disrupting global supply chains and trade flows. Fertilisers, in particular nitrogen inputs, are a clear example of how such disruptions can quickly affect European agricultural production. While overall supply to the EU has not collapsed, repeated crises are exposing its structural fragility.

The conflict in Ukraine has already demonstrated how geopolitical shocks can destabilise fertiliser markets and current tensions risk reinforcing this pattern. These recurring disruptions have led to renewed calls for derogations, including those related to manure application, as farmers seek greater flexibility to cope with input uncertainty and shifting market conditions.
This volatility highlights the need for a regulatory framework that can respond swiftly to current and future disruptions. In this context: 1.
Does the Commission recognise that repeated geopolitical disruptions are structurally destabilising agricultural input markets, including fertilisers?
Is the Commission willing to introduce faster and more flexible derogation mechanisms to respond to such disruptions?
If not, what alternative measures does the Commission propose to address ongoing market volatility and future supply shocks affecting the agricultural sector?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.6.2026) The Commission is aware of the significant pressure that farmers in the EU face due to elevated fertiliser prices. The situation is exacerbated by ongoing tensions in the Middle East. On 19 May 2026, the Commission adopted the Fertiliser Action Plan1, setting out short- and long-term measures to improve fertiliser availability, affordability and resilience.

Short term actions include the mobilisation and possible top-up of the agricultural reserve, liquidity support under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) and greater flexibility for advance payments. Longer term measures focus on strengthening EU production capacity, supporting the uptake of recycled nutrients and low carbon alternatives, and reducing strategic dependencies on imports.

Several measures have already been taken, such as the application of reduced flat 1% mark-up for the default Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) values for fertilisers, the adoption of a Temporary State aid framework2 on 29 April 2026, as well as the temporary suspension of duties for imports of ammonia, urea and other nitrogen fertilisers from countries other than Russia and Belarus, within given quotas3.

Additionally, in February 2026, the Commission provided further flexibility under the Nitrates Directive for certain types of materials derived from manure processing (RENURE)4. Furthermore, as laid down in the Fertiliser Action Plan, the Commission will explore short term measures to facilitate the use of digestates, such as extending the RENURE Act.
